cards.a: ST elevation in 2 neighbouring (contiguous) leads. For example, ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF means an inferior STEMI. Treat it as an emergency — the heart muscle is not getting blood.
cards.q: What ECG finding defines a STEMI?

cards.a: Aspirin 325 mg, chewed, as soon as possible — unless the patient is allergic. Aspirin stops platelets clumping and limits the clot. Then add oxygen only if oxygen is low, nitrates, and reperfusion (PCI or thrombolysis).
cards.q: What is the first drug to give in an acute heart attack (myocardial infarction)?

cards.a: MAP = (systolic blood pressure + 2 x diastolic blood pressure) / 3. Example: BP 120/80 gives MAP = (120 + 160) / 3 = 93 mmHg. MAP is the average pressure driving blood to the organs — a MAP below 65 mmHg is too low in shock.
cards.q: What is the formula for mean arterial pressure (MAP)?

cards.a: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume. Example: heart rate 70 beats per minute x stroke volume 70 mL = 4,900 mL per minute, about 5 litres per minute. If the heart beats faster or pumps more per beat, output rises.
cards.q: What is the formula for cardiac output?

cards.a: 1. ACE inhibitor or ARNI, 2. Beta-blocker, 3. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA, e.g. spironolactone), 4. SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g. dapagliflozin). All 4 together lower death and hospital admissions — do not stop them just because the patient feels better.
cards.q: What are the 4 drug pillars for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?

cards.a: Use the CHA2DS2-VASc score. Anticoagulate if the score is 2 or more in men, or 3 or more in women. The score counts heart failure, high blood pressure, age, diabetes, previous stroke, vascular disease and sex. Atrial fibrillation can cause a clot in the heart that travels to the brain and causes a stroke.
cards.q: When do you anticoagulate a patient with atrial fibrillation?

cards.a: Chest pain, fainting (syncope) on exertion, and breathlessness. The aortic valve is narrowed, so the heart cannot push enough blood out, especially during exercise. A harsh systolic murmur at the right upper chest, radiating to the neck, is typical.
cards.q: What is the classic triad of aortic stenosis?

cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause overall, especially after skin infection or IV drug use. The mitral valve is most often affected in general, the tricuspid valve in IV drug users. Look for fever, a new murmur, and emboli — small clots breaking off to brain, lungs or fingers.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of infective endocarditis, and which valve is most often affected?

cards.a: Widespread (diffuse) ST elevation in most leads, with PR depression. This is different from a heart attack, where ST elevation is in one area only. Treatment is an NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen) plus colchicine, which lowers recurrence.
cards.q: What ECG changes are seen in acute pericarditis, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Emergency = very high blood pressure PLUS organ damage (e.g. chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, kidney failure). Treat in hospital with IV drugs, lowering MAP by only 10-20% in the first hour — do not drop it to normal quickly. Urgency = very high blood pressure with NO organ damage. Treat slowly with oral drugs as an outpatient.
cards.q: What is the difference between hypertensive emergency and hypertensive urgency?

cards.a: FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.70 after a bronchodilator. FEV1 is the air breathed out in the first second, FVC is the total air breathed out. A low ratio means the airways are narrowed and air is trapped. Smoking is the main cause.
cards.q: How is COPD diagnosed on spirometry?

cards.a: Short-acting beta-agonist (albuterol/salbutamol) by nebuliser or inhaler, plus ipratropium, plus a steroid (e.g. prednisolone) early. Give oxygen to keep saturation 94-98%. Magnesium sulfate is added in severe attacks. Steroids take hours to work, so give them early.
cards.q: What is the treatment for an acute asthma attack?

cards.a: It predicts how sick a patient with pneumonia is and whether they need hospital admission. 1 point each for: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate 30 or more, Blood pressure low (systolic <90 or diastolic 60 or less), age 65 or more. Score 0-1: treat at home. Score 2: admit. Score 3 or more: consider ICU.
cards.q: What is CURB-65 used for in pneumonia?

cards.a: Use the Wells score first. If risk is low and D-dimer is negative, PE is unlikely. If risk is high, do a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA). Treatment is anticoagulation (blood thinner) — heparin, then warfarin or a DOAC. A massive PE with low blood pressure needs thrombolysis (clot-busting drug).
cards.q: How do you diagnose and treat a pulmonary embolism (PE)?

cards.a: A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2. PAO2 is the oxygen in the alveoli, PaO2 is the oxygen in arterial blood. A high gradient means oxygen is getting into the lungs but not into the blood — for example in PE, pneumonia or ARDS. A normal gradient is roughly (age / 4) + 4 mmHg.
cards.q: What is the A-a gradient formula, and what does a high value mean?

cards.a: PaO2/FiO2 below 300 mmHg, with bilateral lung infiltrates on chest X-ray and no heart failure explaining it. Below 200 is moderate ARDS, below 100 is severe. FiO2 is the fraction of oxygen breathed in — for example on room air FiO2 is 0.21.
cards.q: What PaO2/FiO2 ratio defines ARDS?

cards.a: It is an exudate if ANY of these are true: pleural fluid protein / serum protein >0.5, pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Transudate (e.g. heart failure) is low protein; exudate (e.g. infection, cancer) is high protein.
cards.q: How do Light's criteria separate transudate from exudate in a pleural effusion?

cards.a: RIPE for 2 months, then RI for 4 months — total 6 months. R = rifampicin, I = isoniazid, P = pyrazinamide, E = ethambutol. Add pyridoxine (vitamin B6) with isoniazid to prevent nerve damage. TB usually affects the upper lobes of the lung.
cards.q: What is the standard treatment for active tuberculosis (TB)?

cards.a: Needle decompression first, then a chest drain. Insert a large needle in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, on the affected side. Tension pneumothorax is air trapped in the chest that squeezes the heart and lungs — the patient is hypotensive, breathless, with trachea pushed away and absent breath sounds.
cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for a tension pneumothorax?

cards.a: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, usually because the upper airway collapses. Signs: loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, morning headache, high blood pressure. Use the STOP-BANG score to screen. Treatment is CPAP — a mask that keeps the airway open with air pressure — plus weight loss and avoiding alcohol/sedatives.
cards.q: What is sleep apnoea, and how is it treated?

cards.a: The normal squamous lining of the lower oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-type lining, after years of acid reflux (GERD). It matters because it can progress to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients need surveillance endoscopy.
cards.q: What is Barrett's oesophagus, and why does it matter?

cards.a: The two main causes are H. pylori infection and NSAIDs. H. pylori is treated with triple therapy: a PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole if allergic to penicillin) for 14 days. Then re-test to confirm the infection is gone.
cards.q: What causes a peptic ulcer, and how is H. pylori treated?

cards.a: Ulcerative colitis: continuous inflammation starting in the rectum, only the colon, bloody diarrhoea, no skip areas. Crohn's: skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus, often the terminal ileum, non-bloody diarrhoea, strictures and fistulas, granulomas on biopsy. Both are inflammatory bowel disease.
cards.q: How do you tell ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease?

cards.a: It grades how severe liver failure is, using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Class A = mild, B = moderate, C = severe. A higher score means worse liver function and higher risk of death — it helps decide about transplant.
cards.q: What is the Child-Pugh score used for in cirrhosis?

cards.a: Infection of ascitic fluid in a patient with cirrhosis, without an obvious source. Diagnose by ascitic fluid neutrophil count (PMN) of 250 cells/mm3 or more. Treat with cefotaxime plus albumin. SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient) of 1.1 g/dL or more points to portal hypertension as the cause of the ascites.
cards.q: What is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: Gallstones and alcohol — together they cause most cases. Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, lipase or amylase more than 3 times the upper limit, and imaging showing pancreatitis. Treatment is IV fluids, pain control, and nothing by mouth initially.
cards.q: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?

cards.a: Charcot's triad = fever + right upper quadrant pain + jaundice. It means cholangitis — infection of the bile ducts, usually from a gallstone blocking the duct. Reynolds' pentad adds confusion and low blood pressure (shock) — that is severe cholangitis and needs urgent antibiotics and bile duct drainage (ERCP).
cards.q: What is Charcot's triad, and what does Reynolds' pentad add?

cards.a: IV octreotide (or terlipressin) plus IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone), plus urgent endoscopy with band ligation. Give blood transfusion carefully — aim for haemoglobin around 7 g/dL, not normal, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens bleeding.
cards.q: What is the first treatment for a variceal bleed in cirrhosis?

cards.a: HBsAg positive = current infection. Anti-HBs positive = immunity (after vaccine or past infection). Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection. HBeAg positive = high infectivity. If HBsAg is positive for more than 6 months, it is chronic hepatitis B.
cards.q: How do you interpret hepatitis B serology?

cards.a: Stop the triggering antibiotic if possible. First-line treatment is fidaxomicin, or oral vancomycin. Do NOT use metronidazole as first line anymore. For severe or recurrent cases, faecal microbiota transplant is used. C. difficile causes watery diarrhoea after antibiotics.
cards.q: What is the treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection?

cards.a: Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L. Example: Na 140, Cl 100, HCO3 24 gives 140 - 124 = 16, which is high. A high anion gap means metabolic acidosis from acids like lactate, ketones (DKA), renal failure or toxins.
cards.q: What is the anion gap formula?

cards.a: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3- + 8, plus or minus 2. It is used in metabolic acidosis to check if the lungs are compensating correctly. Example: HCO3- 12 gives expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26 mmHg. If the actual PaCO2 is much higher, there is also a respiratory acidosis.
cards.q: What is Winter's formula, and what is it used for?

cards.a: pH = 6.1 + log [ HCO3- / (0.03 x PaCO2) ]. HCO3- is bicarbonate, PaCO2 is carbon dioxide pressure. If HCO3- falls, pH falls (metabolic acidosis). If PaCO2 rises, pH falls (respiratory acidosis). Normal pH is 7.35-7.45.
cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for blood pH?

cards.a: FeNa = fractional excretion of sodium. FeNa below 1% means pre-renal AKI — the kidneys are holding on to sodium because blood flow is low (dehydration, heart failure). FeNa above 2% means ATN — the tubules are damaged and cannot reabsorb sodium. FeNa is not reliable if the patient is on diuretics.
cards.q: How does FeNa separate pre-renal AKI from acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?

cards.a: 1. Calcium gluconate IV — protects the heart, does not lower potassium. 2. Insulin + glucose IV — moves potassium into cells. 3. Salbutamol nebuliser and sodium bicarbonate — also shift potassium in. 4. Dialysis if severe or not responding. Always do an ECG first — look for peaked T waves and wide QRS.
cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for high potassium (hyperkalaemia)?

cards.a: No faster than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours (even slower, 4-6, if high risk). Correcting too fast can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome — permanent brain damage. If the patient has seizures from very low sodium, correct faster at first, then slow down.
cards.q: How fast can you safely correct low sodium (hyponatraemia)?

cards.a: Stage 1: GFR 90 or more, with kidney damage. Stage 2: 60-89. Stage 3a: 45-59, 3b: 30-44. Stage 4: 15-29. Stage 5: below 15, or on dialysis — kidney failure. GFR is measured in mL/min/1.73 m2. Lower GFR means worse kidney function.
cards.q: What are the stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD) by GFR?

cards.a: Nephrotic: heavy protein in urine (more than 3.5 g per day), low albumin, swelling (oedema), high cholesterol, frothy urine. Nephritic: blood in urine (red cell casts), high blood pressure, raised creatinine, less protein. Nephrotic loses protein, nephritic is inflamed and bleeds.
cards.q: How do you tell nephrotic from nephritic syndrome?

cards.a: Osmolality = 2 x Na+ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8. All in mg/dL for glucose and BUN, Na+ in mEq/L. Normal is 275-295 mOsm/kg. Example: Na 140, glucose 180, BUN 14 gives 280 + 10 + 5 = 295. A high osmolality with low sodium suggests pseudohyponatraemia or added osmoles like mannitol.
cards.q: What is the formula for serum osmolality?

cards.a: Corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin). Albumin in g/dL, calcium in mg/dL. Example: calcium 8.0, albumin 2.0 gives 8.0 + 0.8 x 2 = 9.6 mg/dL — actually normal. Use this because calcium binds to albumin, so low albumin makes total calcium look falsely low.
cards.q: What is the corrected calcium formula?

cards.a: Glucose over 250 mg/dL, pH below 7.30, bicarbonate below 18, and ketones in blood or urine. It is caused by insulin deficiency, often triggered by infection or missed insulin. Treatment: IV fluids first, then fixed-rate insulin, and replace potassium — check potassium before starting insulin, because insulin lowers it further.
cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

cards.a: DKA: glucose usually 250-600, pH low, ketones present, patient often young with type 1 diabetes. HHS: glucose very high, often over 600, pH near normal, ketones absent or minimal, severe dehydration, patient often older with type 2 diabetes. Both need IV fluids; DKA needs insulin sooner.
cards.q: How do you tell DKA from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)?

cards.a: Diabetes is diagnosed if any one is true: HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour glucose 200 mg/dL or more after a glucose load, or random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms. HbA1c shows average glucose over 2-3 months.
cards.q: What are the diagnostic cut-offs for diabetes?

cards.a: Low cortisol with high ACTH means primary adrenal failure (Addison's disease) — the adrenal gland itself has failed. Low cortisol with low ACTH means secondary — the pituitary is not sending ACTH. Addison's: fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, high potassium, low sodium, and darkening of the skin. Treatment is hydrocortisone, with extra dose in illness.
cards.q: How do you tell primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?

cards.a: Too much cortisol. Causes: long-term steroid use (most common), pituitary tumour (Cushing's disease), adrenal tumour, or ectopic ACTH from a lung cancer. Signs: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple stretch marks, high blood pressure, high glucose, weak muscles, easy bruising.
cards.q: What causes Cushing syndrome, and what does it look like?

cards.a: High calcium (over 10.5 mg/dL) is usually from hyperparathyroidism or cancer. Symptoms: stones (kidney stones), bones (bone pain), groans (abdominal pain, constipation), moans (confusion, depression). Treatment: IV fluids first, then a bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronate). Calcitonin works fast but only for a short time.
cards.q: What causes high calcium, and how is it treated?

cards.a: SIADH: too much ADH, so the body holds water, sodium falls, urine is concentrated, patient is clinically euvolaemic (not dry, not overloaded). Diabetes insipidus: too little ADH (central) or kidneys do not respond to ADH (nephrogenic) — patient makes large amounts of very dilute urine and is very thirsty.
cards.q: How do you tell SIADH from diabetes insipidus?

cards.a: Thyroid storm is life-threatening overactive thyroid: high fever, fast heart rate, confusion, agitation. Treatment: 1. Beta-blocker (propranolol) to slow the heart, 2. Propylthiouracil (PTU) to block new thyroid hormone, 3. Steroids, 4. Iodine — given AFTER the PTU, at least 1 hour later, otherwise iodine feeds hormone production.
cards.q: What is the treatment for thyroid storm, and in what order?

cards.a: It is a tumour of the adrenal medulla that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts. Symptoms: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and very high blood pressure. Diagnose with plasma or urine metanephrines. Treatment: alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) FIRST, then beta-blocker — never beta-blocker alone, because that leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and blood pressure can rise further.
cards.q: What is phaeochromocytoma, and what is the key treatment rule?

cards.a: A serious skin reaction to drugs, with fever, eosinophilia (high eosinophils) and internal organ involvement (liver, kidney). It starts 2-6 weeks after starting a drug like allopurinol, carbamazepine or phenytoin. Stop the drug immediately, give steroids if severe. It is different from a simple drug rash — organs are involved.
cards.q: What is DRESS syndrome?

cards.a: Hypothyroidism: low T4, high TSH, weight gain, cold intolerance, slow heart rate, constipation, fatigue. Treat with levothyroxine. Hyperthyroidism: high T4, low TSH, weight loss, heat intolerance, fast heart rate, tremor, diarrhoea. Treat with methimazole, beta-blocker, and consider radioiodine or surgery.
cards.q: How do thyroid function tests differ in hypo- and hyperthyroidism?

cards.a: Low ferritin is the most reliable test — ferritin below 30 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency in most patients. Also: low haemoglobin, low MCV (small red cells), low iron, high TIBC. Causes: blood loss (especially GI in adults), poor diet, malabsorption. Treat the cause plus oral iron.
cards.q: What lab finding confirms iron deficiency anaemia?

cards.a: B12 deficiency: large red cells (high MCV), low B12, neurological symptoms — numbness, tingling, loss of vibration sense, and dorsal column problems. Folate deficiency: same blood picture, but NO neurological symptoms. Treat B12 with B12 injections or high-dose oral B12; treat folate with folate — but check B12 first, because giving folate alone can worsen B12 nerve damage.
cards.q: How do you tell B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?

cards.a: HbS is abnormal haemoglobin that sickles red cells when oxygen is low. Crises: painful vaso-occlusive crisis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19). Hydroxyurea increases fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises. Patients need vaccinations and penicillin prophylaxis in childhood.
cards.q: What is sickle cell disease, and what does hydroxyurea do?

cards.a: AML is usually in adults, with Auer rods in the blood/bone marrow, and blasts in the blood. ALL is usually in children, with lymphoblasts, and often presents with bone pain and fever. Both present with anaemia, low platelets, low white cells, and infections from bone marrow failure.
cards.q: How do you tell AML from ALL?

cards.a: Hodgkin lymphoma: Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy, often young adults, painless lymph nodes, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), spreads in a predictable pattern. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: more varied, often extranodal, no Reed-Sternberg cells. Both need biopsy, not just imaging.
cards.q: What is the key cell in Hodgkin lymphoma?

cards.a: Prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, and schistocytes (fragmented red cells) on the blood film. It is caused by widespread clotting and bleeding at the same time, often from sepsis, trauma or obstetric catastrophe. Treat the cause, give platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate as needed.
cards.q: What labs are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?

cards.a: TTP: fever, low platelets, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, neurological symptoms, and kidney failure — the pentad. It is due to low ADAMTS13, which normally cuts von Willebrand factor. Treatment is urgent plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) plus steroids. Do NOT give platelets unless there is life-threatening bleeding — they worsen clotting.
cards.q: What is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and what is the treatment?

cards.a: CRAB: C = hyperCalcaemia, R = Renal failure, A = Anaemia, B = Bone lesions (lytic, punched-out lesions on X-ray). It is a plasma cell cancer with monoclonal protein (M-spike) on electrophoresis and Bence Jones protein in urine. Back pain and kidney failure are common presentations.
cards.q: What is the CRAB acronym in multiple myeloma?

cards.a: Warfarin is monitored by INR (target usually 2-3), and reversed with vitamin K or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Heparin is monitored by aPTT, reversed with protamine. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) do not need routine monitoring; apixaban is reversed with andexanet alfa, dabigatran with idarucizumab.
cards.q: How do you monitor and reverse warfarin, heparin and DOACs?

cards.a: Stop the transfusion immediately, check the patient, and send blood samples. Fever alone may be a febrile reaction; fever + low blood pressure + flank pain + dark urine suggests acute haemolytic reaction from ABO mismatch — this is an emergency. TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) causes breathlessness and low oxygen within 6 hours of transfusion.
cards.q: What do you do first in a transfusion reaction, and what is TRALI?

cards.a: 1-hour bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid fluids if hypotensive or lactate 4 or more, and start vasopressors (norepinephrine) if blood pressure stays low. qSOFA of 2 or more (low BP, fast breathing, altered mental state) predicts a bad outcome.
cards.q: What is the 1-hour sepsis bundle?

cards.a: Bacterial: high white cells and protein in CSF, low glucose, high opening pressure. Viral: white cells raised (mostly lymphocytes), protein mildly raised, glucose normal. Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone (given before or with antibiotics), plus ampicillin if age over 50, pregnant, or immunocompromised — to cover Listeria.
cards.q: How does bacterial meningitis differ from viral meningitis on CSF, and what is empiric treatment?

cards.a: CD4 below 200 cells/uL: risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) — give co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. CD4 below 100: toxoplasmosis. CD4 below 50: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and CMV retinitis. ART (antiretroviral therapy) is started regardless of CD4 count, and it reduces opportunistic infections.
cards.q: What opportunistic infections occur at which CD4 counts in HIV?

cards.a: Cellulitis is a spreading skin infection, usually streptococci or Staph aureus, with redness, warmth and pain — treat with flucloxacillin or cephalexin. Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to the skin changes, rapid spread, crepitus (gas in tissue), low blood pressure — needs urgent surgery (debridement) plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
cards.q: How do you tell cellulitis from necrotising fasciitis?

cards.a: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by Ixodes ticks. Stage 1: erythema migrans — a bull's-eye rash. Stage 2: heart block, facial nerve palsy, arthritis. Stage 3: chronic arthritis, skin changes. Treatment: doxycycline for early disease, ceftriaxone for severe late disease.
cards.q: What are the stages of Lyme disease?

cards.a: Primary: painless chancre. Secondary: rash on palms and soles, condyloma lata. Latent: no symptoms but tests positive. Tertiary: gummas, neurosyphilis, cardiovascular disease. Screening is with RPR or VDRL (non-treponemal), confirmed with a treponemal test (FTA-ABS / TP-PA). Treatment is penicillin G.
cards.q: What are the stages of syphilis, and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: A hot, swollen, painful single joint with fever. Aspirate the joint immediately — send for white cell count, Gram stain and culture. Do NOT delay aspiration to wait for blood tests. Treatment is urgent drainage plus IV antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin / vancomycin if MRSA risk). Septic arthritis can destroy a joint in days.
cards.q: What is the emergency action in suspected septic arthritis?

cards.a: MRSA: vancomycin or linezolid. Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem. Anaerobes (e.g. abdominal infection): metronidazole. Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella): macrolide or doxycycline. Always check local resistance patterns and allergies.
cards.q: Which antibiotic covers MRSA, Pseudomonas, anaerobes and atypical pneumonia?

cards.a: Influenza A/B causes fever, cough, myalgia and headache in winter. Complications include secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae). Treatment: oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptoms in high-risk patients. Vaccination is the main prevention, especially in older people and those with chronic disease.
cards.q: What are the features and treatment of influenza?

cards.a: Fever, rigors, low blood pressure and a new heart murmur after a dental procedure or IV drug use. Blood cultures must be taken BEFORE antibiotics — at least 3 sets. Diagnosis uses the Duke criteria (blood cultures, echocardiogram showing vegetation, fever, risk factors, emboli). Treatment is prolonged IV antibiotics for 4-6 weeks.
cards.q: What are the key steps in diagnosing infective endocarditis?

cards.a: Anti-CCP antibody is the most specific test for rheumatoid arthritis. It is often positive years before symptoms. RF (rheumatoid factor) is sensitive but less specific. RA affects MCP and PIP joints symmetrically, spares DIP joints, causes morning stiffness over 1 hour, and can cause erosions and deformity. First-line treatment is methotrexate.
cards.q: What is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis?

cards.a: ANA positive in almost all patients, anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity, anti-Smith is very specific. Signs: malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, arthritis, kidney disease (lupus nephritis), and low complement (C3, C4). Young women are most affected.
cards.q: Which antibodies are used in SLE, and what are the classic signs?

cards.a: Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals of monosodium urate, under polarised light. Pseudogout: rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals of calcium pyrophosphate. Gout usually affects the big toe (podagra), pseudogout usually affects the knee. Treat acute gout with NSAID, colchicine or steroids — do not start allopurinol during an acute attack.
cards.q: How do gout and pseudogout crystals differ under the microscope?

cards.a: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) affects people over 50, with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, and vision loss. It is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica. Start high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY if suspected — do not wait for a biopsy — because vision loss can be permanent. ESR is usually very high.
cards.q: What is giant cell arteritis, and why must steroids be started immediately?

cards.a: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain and stiffness in shoulders and hips in people over 50, high ESR/CRP, no muscle weakness, responds quickly to low-dose steroids. Fibromyalgia: widespread pain and fatigue, tender points, normal labs, no inflammation, sleep disturbance — treat with exercise, sleep hygiene and amitriptyline/duloxetine, not steroids.
cards.q: How do you tell polymyalgia rheumatica from fibromyalgia?

cards.a: HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis. It causes inflammatory back pain in young men, worse in the morning and at night, better with exercise (not rest), sacroiliitis on X-ray, and a stiff spine (bamboo spine) over time. Treatment is NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors.
cards.q: What is HLA-B27 associated with, and what is the pattern of back pain?

cards.a: CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anti-centromere antibody is seen in limited scleroderma (CREST). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is seen in diffuse scleroderma, with lung and kidney involvement. Both cause tight, thickened skin.
cards.q: What is CREST syndrome, and which antibodies are seen in scleroderma?

cards.a: Sjögren's syndrome causes dry eyes and dry mouth, due to autoimmune destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands. Antibodies: anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB). Patients are at increased risk of lymphoma. Use artificial tears and saliva substitutes, and check for other autoimmune diseases.
cards.q: What is Sjögren's syndrome?

cards.a: Osteoarthritis: wear-and-tear, affects weight-bearing joints and DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), pain worse with use, better with rest, no morning stiffness or only briefly, X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes. RA: inflammatory, MCP/PIP, morning stiffness over 1 hour, pain better with use, erosions on X-ray.
cards.q: How do you tell osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?

cards.a: Aspirate the joint. Septic arthritis: very high white cell count in fluid (usually over 50,000), positive Gram stain/culture, needs urgent drainage and antibiotics. Gout: urate crystals, white cells lower, patient may have fever but joint is less hot and the history is typical. Never assume gout — always aspirate a hot joint if infection is possible.
cards.q: How do you tell septic arthritis from gout in a hot, swollen joint?
